chunks: PPA: power, performance, area trade-offs. The question: What is power, performance, area (PPA)? Describe the tradeoffs.
PPA stands for power, performance and area. These are the three numbers that chip designers trade against each other. Performance is how fast the chip does its work.
Power is how much energy it burns. Area is how much silicon it uses, which mostly matters because it sets the cost. You can almost never improve all three at once.
Each design decision moves at least two of them, and the right balance depends on the product.
Think of a delivery company choosing trucks. Speed is performance, fuel is power, and the price of the fleet is area.
A faster truck burns much more fuel, because fuel use climbs faster than speed.
Two slower trucks can carry the same load as one fast truck while burning less fuel in total, but you must buy two trucks.
A phone, a server and a tiny sensor each want a different mix.
Cost grows faster than linearly with die area because fewer dies fit on the wafer and each has a larger chance of containing a defect.
Big dies are therefore broken into chiplets, or redundancy is added, to protect yield.
Performance: how much useful work gets done per second, such as clock speed times work per cycle. Power: energy used per second, from switching plus leakage.
Area: the size of the silicon die, which drives its cost. Yield: the fraction of manufactured chips that work. Larger chips yield worse.
Pipelining: splitting a long logic path into stages so each clock cycle can be shorter. Pareto frontier: the set of designs where improving one metric must worsen another.
A block of logic (circuits that compute an answer) takes 1000 picoseconds (picoseconds, trillionths of a second).
Each pipeline stage adds 60 picoseconds for the register (storage cells) between stages. With 1 stage, the cycle is 1060 picoseconds.
With 8 stages, it is 1000 over 8 plus 60 equals 185 picoseconds. That is a clock 1060 over 185 about 5. 73 times faster, not 8 times, because the fixed overhead stays.
Meanwhile the extra registers add area and clock power. That is the whole idea.
"PPA is power, performance and area, the three axes you trade in chip design. Power is switching, alpha C V squared f, plus leakage.
Performance is speed, frequency times work per cycle. Area is silicon cost. Raising voltage or deepening the pipeline buys speed but costs power or area.
Relaxing timing saves power and area. Which trade you make depends on the product: a phone wants low power, a server wants performance, an IoT chip wants small area."
